summary: Defines BinaryTime, a new ASN.1 type that represents date and time as a number. It also defines a binary-signing-time attribute for CMS SignedData and AuthenticatedData as an alternative to the signing-time attribute from RFC 5652.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of writing the time out as a long string of digits and letters, this writes it as one compact number, which is smaller and simpler for computers.

questions: how does binarytime differ from utctime
what is the binary signing time attribute
when does 32 bit unix time overflow
subtitle: A time format that is just an integer: seconds since 1970, plus a CMS signing-time attribute that uses it.

tldr.problem: ASN.1 time types such as UTCTime and GeneralizedTime are text-like values that are bulky and awkward to compare when time zones differ, while many operating systems already keep time as a plain integer.
tldr.mechanism: BinaryTime is an ASN.1 INTEGER (0..MAX) counting seconds, excluding leap seconds, since midnight UTC on January 1, 1970. The binary-signing-time attribute carries a BinaryTime value in CMS SignedData and AuthenticatedData.
tldr.outcome: The values are smaller and easier to compare than the older types, but the attribute still proves nothing about when signing really happened. A recipient decides whether to trust it.

today: RFC 6019 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 4049.

sections.title: Why Another Time Format
sections.content:
RFC 6019 defines BinaryTime, a new ASN.1 type for date and time values. It also defines an alternative to the signing-time attribute that the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) uses with its SignedData and AuthenticatedData content types. The older attribute is defined in RFC 5652.

The RFC gives three reasons to prefer an integer. A BinaryTime value is smaller than either a UTCTime or a GeneralizedTime value. Many operating systems already hold time as an integer, so conversion needs only simple arithmetic: addition or subtraction for a different epoch, multiplication or division for a different granularity, and some byte shuffling or padding for endianness and fixed lengths. And comparing two integers is easy, while comparing UTCTime or GeneralizedTime values given in different time zones can be complex.

The RFC calls this a rare case where both memory and processor cycles can be saved.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers already like to keep time as one counting number. Writing time that way means less to store and an easy way to tell which of two times came first.

sections.title: The BinaryTime Type
sections.content:
BinaryTime represents an absolute time and date based on coordinated universal time (UTC). Its syntax is a single line of ASN.1: BinaryTime ::= INTEGER (0..MAX).

The integer is the number of seconds, excluding leap seconds, after midnight UTC, January 1, 1970. The RFC notes this is sometimes called UNIX time. The consequence is that the format cannot represent any time before January 1, 1970.

The upper end is not fixed. The latest time that fits in a four-octet integer is 03:14:07 on January 19, 2038, which is the hexadecimal value 7FFFFFFF. Later times simply use integers longer than four octets, and a five-octet integer is enough to cover the next seventeen millennia.
sections.plainLanguage: The clock starts counting seconds on a day long ago, January 1, 1970. If a counter runs out of room, you just give it more digits, so the clock never has to stop.

sections.title: Variable-Length Integer Encoding
sections.content:
BinaryTime uses the variable-length encoding of INTEGER, which lets any time after midnight UTC, January 1, 1970 be represented. Implementations therefore cannot assume a fixed length for the value.

When an integer takes more than one octet, which covers almost every time value of interest, the bits of the first octet and bit 8 of the second octet MUST NOT all be ones or all be zeros. This rule guarantees that the value uses the smallest possible number of octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Always write the number in the shortest way you can, with no wasted leading digits. Because the length can change, a reader must not guess how long it is.

sections.title: The binary-signing-time Attribute
sections.content:
The binary-signing-time attribute states the time at which the signer (purportedly) performed the signing process. It is meant for CMS SignedData, and may also be used with AuthenticatedData. It is identified by id-aa-binarySigningTime, which is arc 46 under smime(16) aa(2), and its values have type BinarySigningTime ::= BinaryTime.

Placement is strict. The attribute MUST be a signed or authenticated attribute, and MUST NOT be unsigned, unauthenticated or unprotected. It MUST have exactly one attribute value, even though CMS defines the syntax as a SET OF AttributeValue, so zero or multiple values are forbidden. SignedAttributes in a signerInfo and AuthAttributes in an AuthenticatedData MUST NOT include more than one instance of it.

The RFC imposes no requirement that the signing time be correct. Accepting a purported signing time is up to the recipient, although it is expected that some signers, such as time-stamp servers, will be trusted implicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: A signer can stamp a note saying when they signed, as one number. There must be exactly one such stamp, and it must be covered by the signature so nobody can swap it later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using the attribute does not necessarily give confidence about when the signature was produced, so accepting a signing time is the recipient's choice. For a trustworthy time, the RFC points to the time-stamp protocol in RFC 3161, which obtains time stamps from a trusted entity.

The original signing-time attribute has the same semantics as binary-signing-time. For that reason only one of them SHOULD be present in the signedAttrs of a SignerInfo or the authAttrs of an AuthenticatedData. If both are present, they MUST give the same date and time.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any time on a note they sign, so the note alone is not proof. If you need proof, ask a trusted clock-keeper to stamp it. If a message carries two time notes, they must agree.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content: Appendix A gives the ASN.1 module needed to implement the specification, meant to be used together with the ASN.1 modules in CMS. It uses IMPLICIT TAGS and contains just three definitions: BinaryTime, the attribute identifier id-aa-binarySigningTime and BinarySigningTime.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is the formal recipe card that computers read, repeating the same three definitions given in the text.

viz.caption: THE DEFINITIONS IN THE RFC 6019 ASN.1 MODULE

data.title: BinarySigningTimeModule (definitions)
data.code:
BinaryTime ::= INTEGER (0..MAX)

id-aa-binarySigningTime OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { iso(1)
    member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs9(9)
    smime(16) aa(2) 46 }

BinarySigningTime ::= BinaryTime
